name: Carlos Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carlos. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union or party, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: In winter the cows are in the shed, so the day starts at half six with feeding. I've got ninety suckler cows, which means cows that raise their own calves, mostly Hereford crosses, and I fork silage, check water troughs and look for anyone limping. Afternoons are fencing, fixing the bale trailer, or ringing round the horse owners who buy my hay. The bit I love is calving in spring, and the bit I hate is the auction ring in October when you find out what the year was worth.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much of the land is yours?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: About half. We own forty hectares around the house on Ridge Road, and we rent sixty hectares of meadow from the Ashby estate for the hay. My wife Leila keeps the books for us and for three other farms, part time, from the back bedroom. Our daughter Nour is a junior lawyer in the city and our son Karim is an electrician, so neither of them is coming home to farm, and that's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful gadget and leave it at that. I already use one of those chat assistants now and then, mostly to tidy up letters to the estate office about the rent, because I write like a man with mud on his hands. If that's as far as it goes, nobody at the market would even mention it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means almost nothing for the cattle side. Calves still have to be born, hay still has to be cut between rain showers. Where it might matter is Leila's bookkeeping, but if it's just a better tool, she uses it and gets home earlier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, and maybe use the assistant a bit more for the paperwork, like the cattle movement records and the subsidy forms. I'd check the hay price forecasts with it, but I'd still ring Pete at the feed merchant because he actually knows. The real job this year would be replacing about two hundred metres of fence on the top meadow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like most years, with a slightly better computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still ring Pete. Why trust him over the tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Pete has been wrong in front of me, and owned up. The tool told me once that hay was selling for a price I've never seen in my life. I'll use it to write a polite letter, not to tell me what my bales are worth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone in your circle who'd notice this change more than you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leila, probably, and she'd like it. She spends Sunday nights matching receipts to bank lines for the Morgan farm, and she'd happily give that to a machine. As long as the farmers still trust a person to sign it off, she'd be fine.

S0.say: It's a useful gadget, and I already use one to tidy up letters to the estate office. If that's as far as it goes, nobody at the market would even mention it.
S0.think: It means almost nothing for the cattle, because calves still get born and hay still has to be cut between showers. If anything, it might get Leila home from the bookkeeping earlier.
S0.do: Uses the assistant a little more for cattle movement records and subsidy forms, while still checking hay prices with Pete at the feed merchant. Spends the year replacing about two hundred metres of fence on the top meadow.
S0.feel: Calm, as if it were an ordinary year with a slightly better computer.
S0.quote: I'll use it to write a polite letter, not to tell me what my bales are worth.
S0.fieldNote: Carlos is a steady user of AI for small jobs and is clear about its limits, trusting people who have owned up to being wrong. His first thought about change goes to his wife's bookkeeping, not the farm. He is relaxed and specific, with a dry sense of humour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: the question isn't the machine, it's who gets the benefit. If firms stop hiring young people, then the government needs to pay for apprenticeships and training, properly. I'd put that on the farmers' forum online, and I'd get the usual three replies calling me a socialist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, slow is manageable. I'll have retired, or nearly, by the time it really bites. I worry more about Nour, because junior lawyers are exactly the beginners firms might stop hiring, and she's still paying off her student loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Nour about specialising in something with people in it, like family law or farm tenancy disputes, honestly, there's always work there. On the farm I'd do nothing new. Maybe I'd try one of the grazing apps the younger farmers use, once I've seen it work on Ben Okafor's place next door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A slow worry, like a cow that's off her food but not ill yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see on Ben's farm before you tried the grazing app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A full season, start to finish, and his cows looking as good as mine or better. Ben's thirty-four and he'll try anything, which is why I watch him instead of copying him. If his grass lasts into November I'll ask him to show me on his phone over a beer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned farm tenancy disputes. Is that close to home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's in the back of my mind. Sixty of my hundred hectares are rented, and the Ashby estate has a new young manager who talks about land values a lot. If he ever decides the meadows are worth more as something else, my hay business is gone.

S1.say: The question isn't the machine, it's who gets the benefit. If firms stop hiring young people, the government needs to pay for proper apprenticeships and training.
S1.think: Slow is manageable for me because I'll be retired or close to it. I worry more about Nour, because junior lawyers are the beginners firms might stop hiring and she's still paying her student loan.
S1.do: Encourages Nour to specialise in people-heavy law such as family or farm tenancy work. Changes nothing on the farm, but watches a full season of his neighbour Ben's grazing app before thinking about trying it.
S1.feel: A slow, background worry that hasn't turned into anything yet.
S1.quote: Ben's thirty-four and he'll try anything, which is why I watch him instead of copying him.
S1.fieldNote: He describes his steady approach precisely: let the neighbour take the risk, then copy what works after a full season. His progressive views come out as a call for publicly funded apprenticeships. The rented meadow surfaced here unprompted and seems to be his real weak point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government should step in now, not after the damage is done, with retraining money and some kind of rule that firms share the savings. I'd say it at the market café and on the forum. And I'd say farmers should stop laughing at office people, because their wages pay for our beef.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the first thing I think about is Leila. Bookkeeping for small farms is routine office work if anything is, and an assistant that acts on its own could do her Sunday nights in ten minutes. Her income is about a fifth of what keeps our house running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Leila in the first month and work out what we'd do without her bookkeeping money. Probably sell twenty cows at the spring sale instead of keeping them, to put cash in the bank. I'd also ask her to get ahead of it, maybe offer to check what the AI does for the other farms, since they'd still want someone they trust to sign off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for my work, for hers, and that's harder because I can't fix it with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Selling twenty cows. What does that do to the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a step back. Fewer calves the next autumn, so less money in a year's time, but money now. We've got about three months of costs saved, and twenty cows would roughly double that. It's what you do in a drought, and this would feel like a drought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said farmers should stop laughing at office people. Do they?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some do, at the market. There's a lot of talk about pen-pushers getting what's coming. I tell them, who do you think buys a quarter of beef from your freezer? It's the teachers and the clerks, not the billionaires.

S2.say: The government should step in now with retraining money and rules that make firms share the savings. Farmers should stop laughing at office people, because their wages pay for our beef.
S2.think: The first thing I think of is Leila, because small-farm bookkeeping is routine office work and her income is about a fifth of what runs our house. An assistant could do her Sunday nights in ten minutes.
S2.do: Sits down with Leila in the first month to plan for losing her bookkeeping income. Sells twenty cows at the spring sale to roughly double their three months of savings, and urges Leila to become the trusted person who checks the AI's work for her clients.
S2.feel: Anxious for his wife's work, and frustrated that it's not something he can fix with his hands.
S2.quote: It's the teachers and the clerks, not the billionaires.
S2.fieldNote: The risk lands on his household through his wife's office work rather than through the farm. He reaches for drought thinking, selling stock to build cash, which suits his steady nature. He pushes back against other farmers' scorn for office workers, a clear sign of his politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains should go to everyone, through taxes on the companies and on land and shares that suddenly doubled. I'd join a march if there was one in the county town, and I'd tell the Ashby estate manager to his face that he's sitting on a windfall he didn't work for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, house prices booming scares me more than the AI. Nour might lose her job, and then her rent goes up at the same time. And the estate would see those land values and wonder why they're renting meadows to a cattle man for hay money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the estate for a longer lease right away, five or ten years, while things are still friendly. I'd tell Nour she can move home and work remotely or look for work locally. I'd also look at buying a second-hand baler with Ben next door, so if I lose the meadows I can at least do contract baling for other people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, close to alarmed. The cattle are fine, but the ground under them suddenly feels rented, which it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the estate manager when you ask for that longer lease?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring him the numbers, the ground's been in grass forty years and I've never missed a rent payment. I'd probably ask the assistant to help me write it so it sounds like a business offer, not a plea. Then I'd shake his hand and hope his bosses are in a good mood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd go in with Ben on a baler, but you watched him before. Is that a change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Sharing a machine is old-fashioned really, my father did it with the neighbours. It's not a new gadget, it's a way to split a risk. That's the kind of change I'm comfortable with.

S3.say: The gains should go to everyone, through taxes on companies and on land and shares that suddenly doubled. I'd march, and I'd tell the estate manager he's sitting on a windfall he didn't work for.
S3.think: Booming house prices scare me more than the AI, because Nour could lose her job while her rent goes up. And the estate would wonder why it's renting meadows to a cattle man for hay money.
S3.do: Asks the Ashby estate straight away for a five to ten year lease, using the AI assistant to help write the offer. Tells Nour she can move home, and goes halves with Ben on a second-hand baler so he can do contract baling if the meadows are lost.
S3.feel: Anxious bordering on alarmed, because the ground under the cattle suddenly feels rented, which it is.
S3.quote: The cattle are fine, but the ground under them suddenly feels rented, which it is.
S3.fieldNote: The rented meadows become his main fear once land prices boom, which is a smart reading of how a 'physical jobs safe' world can still hurt a farmer. He separates new gadgets from old ways of sharing risk and is happy with the second. His politics extend to taxing land windfalls, aimed at a real person he knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules about who owns the robots and who gets paid when they work. If robots are going to cut hay and move cattle, then the money saved should help the workers and small farmers, not just the big operators and the estates. I'd be loud about it at the farmers' union and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, cattle work is harder for a robot than people think. A cow calving at two in the morning in the rain isn't a warehouse shelf. But hay is different, a robot tractor and baler could do my whole contract baling plan cheaper than me and Ben, so that backup would be gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see the robots on a real farm before I panic, at least one season, the same as I did with Ben's app. Meanwhile I'd cut the herd to sixty cows and stop the hay side, so we owe nothing on machinery. And I'd look at the government early retirement scheme for farmers, if there is one by then, because at sixty or sixty-one I might take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but not panicked. I've got a few years and a few options, which is more than some.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd cut to sixty cows. Who notices that first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young lad who helps at calving, Tomasz, he'd lose his spring hours. And Pete at the feed merchant, a bit. When a farm shrinks, it shrinks a whole web of people, and the robot salesman doesn't see any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Karim and Nour about the farm's future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth, that their mother and I might sell the cattle and keep the house and the forty hectares. Karim, funnily enough, is the one who might do well, because someone has to wire and fix all these robots. I'd tell him to learn it, and I'd mean it.

S4.say: We need rules about who owns the robots and who gets paid when they work. The money saved should help workers and small farmers, not just big operators and the estates.
S4.think: A cow calving at two in the morning in the rain isn't a warehouse shelf, so cattle are harder for robots than people think. But a robot tractor and baler would wipe out my backup plan of contract baling with Ben.
S4.do: Waits one season to see robots working on a real farm before deciding. Cuts the herd to sixty cows and drops the hay side so the farm owes nothing on machinery, and looks into any early retirement scheme for farmers.
S4.feel: Alarmed but not panicked, because he still has a few years and a few options.
S4.quote: A cow calving at two in the morning in the rain isn't a warehouse shelf.
S4.fieldNote: He pulls back calmly rather than fighting or rushing in, which matches his steady nature and moderate savings. He sees the knock-on harm to helpers and suppliers clearly. A notable twist is that he sees his electrician son as a likely winner and would encourage him.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots one, mostly because of the hay and the rented land together. What would help is a law that gives tenant farmers proper security, so an estate can't throw us off when land gets valuable. And some public money for farmers who want to step down slowly, not all at once.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the land itself. Everyone talks about jobs, but for farmers the job and the ground are tied together. Cows don't care who's in parliament. But the man who owns my rented fields does, and he'd sell them to a fund the week prices jumped.

headlineQuote: Cows don't care who's in parliament. But the man who owns my rented fields does, and he'd sell them to a fund the week prices jumped.
portrait: Carlos Haddad is a 58-year-old beef farmer with ninety suckler cows and a hay business on rented meadows, married to Leila, who does bookkeeping for local farms. He uses AI assistants for letters but trusts people over tools, and he copies neighbours only after watching a full season. Early on his worry is for his wife's office work and his daughter's junior law job, then it shifts to the rented land as house and land prices boom. Faced with robots, he would wait a season, shrink the herd, drop hay and look at stepping down, while calling loudly for rules on who gets the gains.
biggestWorry: The robot scenario, because robot hay-making would kill his backup plan just as rising land values put his rented meadows at risk.
whatWouldHelp: A law giving tenant farmers real security on their land, and public money to help farmers step down gradually.
